summary: Introduces the Advanced Unidirectional Route Assessment metric and measurement method, built on the IP Performance Metrics framework of RFC 2330. It updates RFC 2330's path terminology to allow for parallel subpaths between a source and destination, which arise with multipath technologies.

eli5.summary: Instead of assuming there is one road between two cities, this measures all the roads that traffic might take.

questions: how does paris traceroute find multiple paths
what is a member route in ippm
subtitle: A route metric that describes the whole set of paths between two hosts, not just one.

tldr.problem: The IPPM framework's old "route" metric assumed a single path, but real networks use parallel paths (ECMP and UCMP), and tools like traceroute can only discover hops over a time interval.
tldr.mechanism: AURA defines a Route Ensemble, the set of distinct Member Routes taken by different flows from Src to Dst, built from per-hop records, and describes active, hybrid and combined methods for measuring it.
tldr.outcome: It adds a new Route metric to the IPPM set and updates the path terminology of RFC 2330 to allow parallel subpaths.

facts.label: MPLS paths traceable at a router

today: RFC 9198 is a Proposed Standard from May 2022 that updates RFC 2330, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What Was Wrong With the Old Route Metric
sections.content:
The IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) framework in RFC 2330 includes a simple example metric: the route is "the path, as defined in Section 5, from A to B at a given time". RFC 9198 takes up the challenge of turning that into a proper metric, and specifies two frameworks of measurement methods (active and hybrid active-passive), plus Round-Trip Delay and link discovery from the results.

It lists what the old definition missed:

  • Time: tools like Paris-traceroute need several packets because they rely on Hop Limits, so a route is assessed over an interval.
  • Type-P: routing can depend on the packet type, so the route is assessed for a specific packet type.
  • Parallel paths: ECMP and UCMP create parallel subpaths.
  • Cloud subpaths: some hosts do not decrement the Hop Limit, and tunnels hide hops.
  • Hop: only discoverable and cooperating hosts reveal both link and host information.

All route measurements are limited by how willing hosts along the path are to be discovered.
sections.eli5: The old idea said there is just one road between two places. But there are many roads, some are hidden in tunnels, and you only see them by sending lots of test cars.

sections.title: Scope and Non-Goals
sections.content:
The scope is to define Route metrics that identify the path taken by a packet or a flow between two hosts, built to be usable in other network domains too. The RFC also covers a framework for active methods based on Paris-traceroute-style techniques, and one for hybrid methods such as the Hybrid Type I method that RFC 9197 (IOAM) describes. Hybrid methods are intended only for single administrative domains that offer a way to interrogate nodes on the path. Combinations of the two are in scope.

It formally updates Section 5 of RFC 2330, in path terminology and path description, mainly to allow parallel subpaths between a Source and Destination.

There are explicit non-goals. It does not assess the reverse path from a hop back to the measuring host. The reverse-path delay is that of ICMP packets and may differ from UDP or TCP, and the delay includes unknown processing time at the host that generates the response. So ICMP-based active methods are not supposed to give accurate, reproducible estimates of the delay UDP or TCP will see.
sections.eli5: AURA looks at the outbound trip and finds the hops. It does not promise to know the way back, and it does not promise perfect timing.

sections.title: Hosts, Nodes and Hops
sections.content:
A Host is as in RFC 2330, including routers. A Node is any network function on the path capable of IP-layer communication. The Node identity is the unique address a node uses, such as its globally routable IP address.

Two kinds of node can be found. A Discoverable Node reveals its identity as the requirements of its network demand, for IP by sending the ICMP Time Exceeded message when it drops a packet for TTL or Hop Limit exceeded (as RFC 1122 requires). A Cooperating Node answers direct queries under a previously agreed interrogation protocol and SHOULD also give details such as arrival or departure interface and arrival timestamp.

A Hop specification MUST contain a Node identity and MAY contain arrival and departure interface identification, Round-Trip Delay and an arrival timestamp. A Routing Class is a route that treats a class of different packet types, designated C, equally.

The formal name of the metric is Type-P-Route-Ensemble-Method-Variant, abbreviated Route Ensemble.
sections.eli5: Some stops announce themselves when a car runs out of travel time. Others answer if you knock with the right secret knock. Both kinds help you map the road.

sections.title: Route Ensembles and Member Routes
sections.content:
The REQUIRED parameters include Src and Dst, the hop limit i up to MaxHops, the interval T0 to Tf, a maximum wait Tmax for replies, and F, the number of flows simulated. A flow is the stream of packets with the same n-tuple of header fields that gets identical treatment in a multipath decision.

The metric's building block is a singleton, a Hop specification h(i,j): the identity of the node i hops from Src on Route j. It MUST contain a Node identity and MAY carry arrival interface a(i,j), departure interface d(i,j), an arrival timestamp t(i,j), and Round-Trip Delay measurements.

A single route taken by a single flow is a Member Route: an ordered list {h(1,j), ... h(Nj,j)} ending at Dst. Member Routes in an ensemble must be unique, so two of them differ in hop count or in at least one hop. The Route Ensemble is the aggregate of all distinct Member Routes found between Src and Dst during the interval. Some hops may be empty (null) if nodes do not reply, and member routes may overlap.

For delay and loss, RTD(i,j,T) is a singleton of the Round-Trip Delay of RFC 2681 and RTL(i,j,T) one of the Round-Trip Loss of RFC 6673.
sections.eli5: One car's list of stops is a route. All the different routes cars took, collected together, are the ensemble.

sections.title: Active Measurement Methods
sections.content:
Active methods, which can cross multiple administrative domains, rely on the TTL or Hop Limit Exceeded reaction. They assume flow-based ECMP, since flow hashing avoids packet reordering and extra delay variation (RFC 2991). Early traceroute tools were inaccurate because they kept no flow state. Evolved tools, Paris-traceroute and Scamper, expect ECMP and repeat complete traceroutes with different flow parameters (Paris-traceroute has an "exhaustive" mode, Scamper has "tracelb") to uncover the many available paths.

The trick is to keep the critical header fields constant so every probe looks like the same flow. For IPv6 that means Source, Destination and Flow Label (RFC 6437), and Extension Headers SHOULD be avoided. For IPv4 it means the addresses, protocol number and Diffserv fields plus the first 4 payload bytes, which include ports and ICMP type, code and checksum. Probes may use arbitrary bytes in the ICMP data field to keep the checksum constant. Hops and attempts are told apart by the IP identification field (and the ICMP sequence number in the ICMP case).

Repetitive systems SHOULD occasionally recheck stable path portions, SHOULD keep testing portions that showed ECMP, and SHALL trigger reassessment of the whole Route Ensemble if a hop changes for a previously tested flow. The RFC also describes using a Routing Class C, learned by testing with multiple flows, to cut the number of flows needed, and to investigate delay seen from an intermediate observation point.
sections.eli5: To trace every road, you send test cars that all look the same to the traffic sorters, then change one detail on purpose to see which road each variant takes.

sections.title: Hybrid and Combined Methods
sections.content:
Hybrid Type I methods are an alternative: nodes in the measured domain store the identity of nodes visited, in order, in header data fields, and support a "Loopback" capability that returns a copy of the packet to the encapsulating node. They can also record ingress and egress interfaces, absolute time and generic data, and can identify links without IP addresses, such as links in a LACP bundle or unnumbered interfaces. The packet specification for such a method will likely be only partial.

Combining both kinds can give a more complete view, for example when a node is Cooperating but not Discoverable. For that, nodes at the ingress and egress of an interrogation domain SHOULD be both Discoverable and Cooperating, and nodes that are both SHOULD reveal the same identity to both kinds of method. Ordinary Internet users usually cannot interrogate other networks' OAM, but an operator could combine results from its own access domain with measurements of the path outside it.

Appendix A adds MPLS: an MPLS traceroute using RFC 8029 can check how packets are spread over equal-cost paths at a router, and the minimum number of equivalent MPLS paths traceable at a router should be 32.
sections.eli5: One way is to knock on each door and wait for the answer. The other is to ask a travelling guest to write down each stop. Using both gives a better map.

sections.title: Round-Trip Delay Analysis
sections.content:
Beyond finding hops, delay can hint at what a link is. The RFC lists intercontinental submarine links, satellite communications, congestion and inter-domain paths, and stresses this is an inference. As examples it gives round-trip delay on the order of 100 ms on transatlantic hops, and typically higher than 480 ms across a geostationary satellite hop.

One RTD sample only shows the queue at that instant, so the method takes many samples in a time window W and computes quartiles per hop: minimum, Q1, median Q2, Q3 and maximum. Spread-apart measurements, a growing Interquartile Range (IQR), suggest congestion. The P2 algorithm updates quartiles on the fly as each measurement arrives, saving memory and time compared with methods that need the whole data set.

A hop is identified by the origin address of the ICMP Time Exceeded packet and the TTL distance. Because different return paths exist, the 5-tuple of origin IP, destination IP, reply IP, distance and response TTL or Hop Limit identifies every measurement. The response TTL is normally initialized to 64, 128 or 255.
sections.eli5: One stopwatch reading can be unlucky, so you time the trip many times and look at the spread. If the times jump around a lot, the road is probably crowded.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The considerations for any active measurement of live paths apply here, with pointers to RFC 4656 and RFC 5357. Changing fields to keep checksums identical needs no special security thought, as it is part of synthetic traffic generation designed to have minimal to zero impact on ECMP processing.

Protocols such as ICMP lack cryptographic protection of the data they return, so there are risks in processing untrusted data, but these are limits of existing protocols. For hybrid methods, the security considerations of RFC 9197 apply.

On privacy, active techniques greatly reduce the sensitive information available to observers, while passive observation of user traffic raises many issues. The RFC points readers to the LMAP framework (RFC 7594). There are no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: The test cars are made-up traffic, not anyone's real mail, so they reveal little. But the signs they read along the way are not locked, so the answers can be faked.

data.title: Advanced traceroute with quartiles
data.code:
input:  W (window time of the measurement)
        i_t (time between two measurements)
        E (True: exhaustive, False: a single path)
        Dst (destination IP address)
output: Qs (quartiles for every Hop and Alt)

T := start_timer(W)
while T is not finished do:
|   start_timer(i_t)
|   RTD(Hop,Alt) = advanced-traceroute(Dst,E)
|   for each Hop and Alt in RTD do:
|   |   Qs[Dst,Hop,Alt] := ComputeQs(RTD(Hop,Alt))
|   done
|   wait until i_t timer is expired
done
return (Qs)
